I need to make a decision in this Monopoly turn.

I just completed the GREEN monopoly. I have $461 cash and own seven properties with no houses.

I will mortgage Kentucky, Mediterranean, and Connecticut to raise cash for building three houses on the greens. Ventnor stays unmortgaged as a buffer. The bank has 11 houses and 12 hotels remaining.

Mortgaging three properties yields $200, raising cash to $661. Three houses on the greens cost $600, leaving a tight $61 buffer. I am checking whether p3's pink properties at four houses each pose enough rent risk.

P3's pink properties at four houses each charge $700 on Virginia, $625 on States, and $625 on St Charles. The orange properties are at two houses.

Orange property rent at two houses is manageable. Dark blue and railroad risks are minor. I still need $139 to build three houses.

Mortgaging Kentucky and Mediterranean yields only $140, leaving just $1 after building three houses. That is too risky. Connecticut's $60 mortgage plus Kentucky's $110 gives a safer $61 buffer. I am now checking which spaces I will land on from Kentucky next turn.

I mapped the board positions and confirmed I am on Kentucky Avenue. I am checking whether this is my landing spot or the start of the post-turn phase.

The turn index is 97, but the public timeline ends at turn 96. This suggests my roll may not have registered yet, which conflicts with the POST_TURN_ACTION_DECISION label.

I was released from jail on turn 93 and landed on Virginia. Turns 94 through 96 were other players. Turn 97 is mine, yet the action label reads POST_TURN_ACTION_DECISION. This suggests I may have already taken actions this turn that are not yet visible.

I am now certain this is the optional post-turn actions phase. I must have rolled a 7 from Virginia to reach Kentucky, which would have passed GO.

I am now certain I should build houses on the greens. The bank has only eleven houses remaining, and p3 already holds twelve on the pinks while p1 holds six on the oranges. Opponents are hoarding buildings, so I must act quickly to secure my win condition.

P3 has only $171 cash, so they cannot afford to upgrade their pinks to hotels without mortgaging their four railroads first. If they do upgrade, the returned houses would ease the supply shortage, but that is uncertain.

I will build two houses on the greens now. One house on each property costs $400, leaving a $61 buffer. Rent jumps from roughly $130 to $390 per property once the first house is placed. Three houses would cost $1800 total, which is impossible with my current cash.

Mortgaging all non-green properties would yield only $250, leaving a $739 shortfall for six houses. Even with that cash, the first house on each green only raises rent by about $78 to $94. The real danger is three houses, which would destroy opponents. I am now weighing whether to drain my cash to just $1–$61 for one house each.

I mapped the spaces reachable from Kentucky. Indiana, Illinois, and Water Works are mortgaged. Ventnor is mine. The B&O Railroad costs $200. A roll of 5 would bankrupt me with only $61 cash. I must mortgage the B&O or another property to survive.

I realized that mortgaging the greens before building would waste the houses. Selling them later returns only half their cost, so I must keep mortgage capacity as a buffer. I will build modestly and preserve emergency liquidity instead of mortgaging everything now.

I calculated the exact liquidity trade-offs. Building two houses leaves only $61 cash and a $250 mortgage buffer, which is too thin to survive a $700 pink rent or a $600 brown rent. Building one house yields $261 cash plus the same $250 buffer, giving $511 total liquidity that can handle most risks except the four-house pinks. I am now weighing whether to build zero houses and wait for more cash, since the bank has only eleven houses remaining.

I checked the other players' ability to build. p4 has only $74 and cannot afford dark blue houses without mortgaging everything else. p1 has just $13, so they cannot upgrade their oranges either. p3 can afford to build on the pinks, but they already hold four houses there and would need to upgrade to hotels.

P3 can upgrade one pink property to a hotel for $100, which returns four houses to the bank. This would ease the housing shortage and reduce their cash to $71. The strategic value of building one house on the greens is low because rent only rises to about $130.

I rejected building one house because the $130 rent is too weak and the $61 cash buffer is too thin. Two houses would leave only $311 liquidity, which is still insufficient. I will wait to build until I can reach the three-house tier in a single turn, or at least place two houses on each green property.

I calculated that mortgaging all non-green properties still leaves only $711, which is $89 short of four houses. Even with every mortgage, I could only afford three houses and would retain just $111 in cash. That buffer is too thin to survive a pink property rent of $625 or $700, especially after landing on Chance or a railroad next turn. I will not build houses now; I will wait until I can make a meaningful jump or until the housing supply becomes urgent.

P3's hotel upgrade would return four houses to the bank, not consume them. P4 could reshuffle existing houses to afford one new house, but that would not reduce the overall supply. P1 cannot build on the oranges because their mortgaged properties require expensive unmortgage payments.

No opponent can immediately claim the eleven houses, so building now is a poor move. I am now evaluating trade offers. Indiana would help p3 complete the red set, which I want to block. Marvin and Vermont are mortgaged and could complete my yellow set with Ventnor and Atlantic.

The light blue set is incomplete because Oriental and Baltic are unowned. The red set is split across three players, so completing it is impractical. P4 already holds a dark blue monopoly with houses, making them a dangerous target. P3's four-railroad pink monopoly is the biggest threat. I am now looking for a trade that would give me cash to build three houses or a cheaper second monopoly. Yellow houses cost $150 each.

The light blue set is now the main focus. Oriental and Vermont are unowned, so I must land on them to claim them. With Connecticut already owned, completing the set would give me a cheap-to-develop monopoly with $50 houses that could generate steady cash.

Unmortgaging Vermont would cost $55, which is reasonable. p1 has only $13 and owns an orange monopoly with two houses, so they are desperate but will not break that income stream. They previously rejected offers for Marvin, Indiana, and Vermont, so a better trade is unlikely.

I rejected partial trades for just Marvin or Vermont because they would not fund green house building. A red set trade with p3 is impossible since Indiana belongs to p1. P4 will not break their dark blue monopoly. Only p3 has enough cash to pay, but I cannot extract money from them without giving up something dangerous.

I cannot trade Kentucky to p3 because it serves as a mortgage buffer and blocks their red monopoly. Connecticut and Ventnor block the light blue and yellow sets, so trading them would help opponents more than me. I am now considering whether p3 would pay a large sum for Kentucky to complete their red set.

No trade offers would help me build houses or improve my position. I will end the turn without building and preserve my cash. I am now checking whether this is before or after my roll.

I confirmed this is the post-turn phase after rolling. I have already landed on Kentucky, so ending the turn is correct and necessary.

The $461 cash balance is consistent with a prior roll of seven spaces from Virginia to Kentucky, confirming this is the post-landing phase. I am now reconsidering whether to build one house on each green property anyway, purely for strategic pressure.

Mortgaging Kentucky and Mediterranean Avenue for $140 would leave only $1 cash after building three houses. Unmortgaging later costs an extra $14. With that near-zero balance, any rent would force house sales at a 50% loss. A roll of five on B&O would bankrupt me. A roll of six on Atlantic would send me to auction because I cannot afford it. The safest rolls are two, four, seven, and ten.

I calculated the exact dice probabilities. Sixteen of thirty-six rolls are dangerous, roughly forty-four percent. A roll of two, four, five, six, or ten would force house sales at a fifty percent loss. Only seven, eight, nine, eleven, and twelve are safe. Even a roll of ten lands on jail, which costs fifty dollars to leave.

Building one house would leave $261, which is barely enough to survive a $200 railroad rent. The expected rent gain from that single house is only about $78, and opponents would likely land on it just once before my next turn. That is too weak a return for the $200 cost.

The jump from zero to one house is the worst return on investment. Reaching two houses would yield about $390 in rent, while three would yield roughly $900. I need $739 more to make that leap. Income from opponent landings is too slow to close that gap quickly. P3 remains the biggest threat with four houses on the pink properties.

I will not mortgage anything. I will end the turn without building. I will send a brief strategic public message.
